detail.abstract: The failing firm defence (FFD), while formally recognised in EU merger control, has proven to be practically marginal. This reflects the merger control's typical aversion to concentration that privileges static price competition over dynamic efficiency, capital reallocation, and long-run competitiveness. Drawing on recent economic research, this article reconceptualises the FFD as a mechanism for facilitating efficient exit in a second-best institutional environment. It shows that, where inefficient firms persist, merger control that blocks exit-facilitating transactions can entrench capital misallocation and weaken investment incentives. A reinvigorated FFD would improve the quality of EU merger control while contributing to faster reallocation of capital and enhanced competitiveness of the European economy. This reform requires no change in legal standards, but a shift in analytical emphasis toward dynamic welfare effects.

title: Optimizing Information Asset Investment Strategies in the Exploratory Phase of the Oil and Gas Industry: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
affiliations: Independent, University Institute of Lisbon (IUL) - ISCTE and

detail.title: Optimizing Information Asset Investment Strategies in the Exploratory Phase of the Oil and Gas Industry: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Our work investigates the economic efficiency of the prevailing "ladder-step" investment strategy in oil and gas exploration, which advocates for the incremental acquisition of geological information throughout the project lifecycle. By employing a multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework, we model an alternative strategy that prioritizes the early acquisition of high-quality information assets. We simulate the entire upstream value chain-comprising competitive bidding, exploration, and development phases-to evaluate the economic impact of this approach relative to traditional methods. Our results demonstrate that front-loading information investment significantly reduces the costs associated with redundant data acquisition and enhances the precision of reserve valuation. Specifically, we find that the alternative strategy outperforms traditional methods in highly competitive environments by mitigating the "winner's curse" through more accurate bidding. Furthermore, the economic benefits are most pronounced during the development phase, where superior data quality minimizes capital misallocation. These findings suggest that optimal investment timing is structurally dependent on market competition rather than solely on price volatility, offering a new paradigm for capital allocation in extractive industries.

title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Trade Policy: A Quantitative Analysis
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Economics, Singapore Management University - School of Economics, Singapore Management University - School of Economics and East China Normal University (ECNU)

detail.title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Trade Policy: A Quantitative Analysis
detail.abstract: The European Union (EU) has introduced the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to curb carbon leakage and incentivize global climate policy alignment. We develop a multi-country, multi-sector general equilibrium model featuring input-output linkages, carbon supply chains, and global emission externalities to evaluate the environmental and economic impacts of the EU's CBAM. Our results show that unilateral implementation modestly reduces global emissions due to carbon leakage through global energy markets. Global welfare improves marginally when environmental benefits are accounted for. When other countries respond optimally, strategic carbon policy adjustments under a non-cooperative Nash equilibrium enhance global emission reductions by mitigating both carbon leakage and free-riding. Under a cooperative equilibrium with Nash bargaining, multilateral negotiations yield substantial welfare and environmental gains, with the CBAM functioning as an effective enforcement device that raises the cost of disagreement and fosters deeper global climate cooperation.

title: Paying Voters: Electoral Handouts and Client Commitment
affiliations: Department of Political Science, Yale University

detail.title: Paying Voters: Electoral Handouts and Client Commitment
detail.abstract: Why do candidates distribute pre-election handouts in the absence of vote monitoring? I posit a formal explanation for why electoral candidates in certain low-income countries distribute resources prior to the election even though there is no guarantee that voters will respond to the transfers by voting in their favour. Substantial empirical evidence demonstrates that despite the existence of ballot secrecy laws, the lack of contract enforcement is not a deterrent to the "money for votes" strategy (distribution of electoral handouts) being utilised in many developing polities. To reconcile this fact with the "commitment problem" of the contingent exchange implied in electoral clientelism, I show that pre-election transfers may be a signalling mechanism to indicate candidate strength in order to capture the vote and act as a more effective electoral strategy than programmatic competition for candidates in environments where perceived electoral viability is more important than ideological differences. In contrast to previous literature highlighting the prevalence of poor voters as the critical factor in vote-buying, the model identifies strategic voting in the informal sector as the mechanism by which pre-election handouts are effective in capturing votes.

title: Who Stays, Who Switches: Tax Frictions and the Shift from Mutual Funds
affiliations: Columbia University

detail.title: Who Stays, Who Switches: Tax Frictions and the Shift from Mutual Funds
detail.abstract: This paper shows that unrealized capital gains generate both persistence and fragility in mutual funds. Using newly compiled fund-level data on unrealized gains from SEC filings, I document how investors decide to stay in a mutual fund or switch to lower-fee, tax-efficient vehicles such as separately managed accounts and exchange-traded funds. Unrealized gains create persistence by locking investors into funds despite higher fees and tax disadvantages, as switching triggers immediate capital gains taxes. I show unrealized gains reduce outflows and enable managers to charge higher fees. However, unrealized gains also create fragility through capital gains distributions: when some investors redeem shares, and the fund liquidates appreciated securities, these realized gains are passed through as taxable income to remaining investors. This creates strategic complementarities in which one investor's redemption and switching decision affects others' incentives to stay or switch. I rationalize these dynamics through a bank-run model with heterogeneous unrealized gains and endogenous distributions that generates multiple equilibria under identical fundamentals that creates financial fragility.

title: People as the Compass: A Reflection on the Nature of Finance, Monetary Sovereignty, and Common Prosperity

detail.title: People as the Compass: A Reflection on the Nature of Finance, Monetary Sovereignty, and Common Prosperity
detail.abstract: This paper conducts a groundbreaking economic and philosophical reflection rooted in people’s livelihood predicaments, with the "people-centered" principle as its core value anchor. It directly addresses the key dilemmas: financial and monetary idleness, pressure from rigid livelihood expenditures, the superimposition of local government debt and household mortgage overdrafts, and financial alienation. Subverting Western dogmas of "monetary neutrality" and "the inherent sin of inflation", the paper reconstructs the essential understanding of China’s finance and currency: monetary sovereignty is the ultimate governance resource of the state; a 3.5% moderate inflation rate can serve as a programmable social distribution tool, with 100% of seigniorage income directed into people’s livelihood accounts to alleviate residents’ burdens. Real estate credit expansion represents a "bloated growth" driven by the overdraft of residents’ future consumption, while the fundamental nature of finance lies in being an extension of national governance, the lifeblood of the real economy, and a tool for people’s well-being. The paper innovatively designs a closed-loop debt restructuring scheme of "targeted subsidies for high-mortgage households + central bank currency cancellation", realizing targeted detoxification, restoration of residents’ balance sheets, stabilization of total monetary volume, and avoidance of systemic risks. Using the Chinese metaphors of "heading south with the cart pointing north" and "yuan (compass), zhe (path), dao (essence), shu (method)", the paper elevates the argument to establish "peoplehood" as the fundamental direction of China’s finance. It emphasizes that reconstructing distribution rules through monetary sovereignty is the core path to achieving common prosperity and consolidating the legitimacy of national governance, highlighting the advantages of China’s system and the unique value of indigenous economic philosophy.

title: AgentAssistX: An Agentic Generative AI Framework for Real-Time Life & LTC Insurance Advisory, Risk Scoring, and Compliance Validation in Cloud-Native Environments

detail.title: AgentAssistX: An Agentic Generative AI Framework for Real-Time Life & LTC Insurance Advisory, Risk Scoring, and Compliance Validation in Cloud-Native Environments
detail.abstract: Advanced, real-time risk assessment and advising solutions that enable transparency, compliance, and customer-focused decisionmaking are needed as LTC and life insurance markets become increasingly complex. Manual workflows, lack of personalization, and disconnected regulatory validation hamper traditional advice and underwriting. An AI platform called AgentAssistX may incorporate cloudnative capabilities, including automatic compliance validation, real-time policy advising, and dynamic risk rating. The mixed-methods study combined data from a Google Forms survey of insurance stakeholders (n=10 questions) and a secondary literature review on AI-driven insurance systems, agentic architectures, and cloud-native deployment strategies. Agentic AI and cloud-native infrastructures enable scalability, transparency, and reliability for regulatory insurance domains, according to research. AI-enhanced advising, risk grading, and automated regulatory checks are desired by survey respondents. AgentAssistX uses generic advisory agents, autonomous risk scorers, compliance validation agents, and a cloud-native orchestration layer for security, explainability, and modularity. The paper states that AgentAssistX can cover insurance technology gaps and enable regulatory sandbox trials, advanced explainable AI, and pilot testing.

title: A Unified Framework for Anomalies based on Daily Returns
affiliations: Fordham university, University of Applied Sciences Bremen - School of International Business Bremen, John von Neumann University, Griffith University, Griffith University and MBS School of Business

detail.title: A Unified Framework for Anomalies based on Daily Returns

declarations.funderStatement: Adam Zaremba acknowledges the support of the National Science Center of Poland [Grant No. 2022/45/B/HS4/00451].

detail.abstract: Numerous cross-sectional equity anomalies draw on the same underlying information: the sequence of daily returns over the previous month. Using a data-driven approach, we estimate the empirical mapping from the distribution of last month's daily returns to future performance without imposing functional forms. The resulting Daily Return Information Factor (DRIF) earns economically large premia, holds across subsamples and research designs, and remains significant after controlling for the modern factor zoo. DRIF subsumes most short-horizon and lottery-style anomalies and emerges as a key factor in asset pricing tests.

title: Political Identity and Conjunction Fallacy: Experimental Evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Economics, Jinan University - Institute for Economic and Social Research, Renmin University of China and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Political Identity and Conjunction Fallacy: Experimental Evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
detail.abstract: In the context of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, experimental participants evaluate lotteries based on electoral outcomes (Trump or Harris winning), economic outcomes (improvement or decline), and the conjunctions of these outcomes. We document a conjunction fallacy in choices: participants value lotteries on conjunctive events more than single events. This pattern is stronger when conjunctive outcomes are congruent with participants' partisan identities--for example, a Harris victory combined with improved economic condition for Democrats--than when they are incongruent. Our results challenge models that satisfy dominance and point to preference-based explanations encompassing the source and the valence of uncertainty.

title: Corporate Responsibility, Governance, and National Competitiveness in India: A Policy-Oriented Review

detail.title: Corporate Responsibility, Governance, and National Competitiveness in India: A Policy-Oriented Review

detail.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) and governance have assumed increasing importance in India's economic and policy landscape, particularly following regulatory mandates and competitiveness-driven reforms. This paper presents a policy-oriented review of CSR, stakeholder engagement, governance practices, and their relationship with national competitiveness in India. Drawing on empirical studies, policy reports, and comparative analyses, the paper examines how responsible corporate behavior contributes to organizational performance, social accountability, and economic confidence. A conceptual linkage between corporate responsibility and national competitiveness is developed, highlighting the role of governance quality, stakeholder trust, and institutional frameworks. The paper offers policy-relevant insights for strengthening India's corporate ecosystem in alignment with long-term developmental objectives and the vision of Viksit Bharat (Developed India by 2047).

title: Capital Adjustment Costs and Stranded Assets in an Optimal Energy Transition
affiliations: Humboldt University Berlin, World Bank and Vienna University of Technology

detail.title: Capital Adjustment Costs and Stranded Assets in an Optimal Energy Transition

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: In the context of a green energy transition, capital adjustment costs render effective substitution between clean and dirty energy sources finite and endogenous, despite infinite long-run substitutability. Ramsey optimal paths robustly frontload clean investment before exhaustion of a given carbon budget, but also generally imply some capital stranding. Along the path of emissions reduction, new investment is quantitatively more important than reduced output or labor redeployment. An ambitious climate goal in our benchmark calibration implies modest levels of stranded capital at 1.5% of GDP, but this rises to more than 7% if implementation is delayed by a decade.

title: (No) Opportunities for Redistributive Policies? - Voting Behavior and Cross-Pressures Between Economic and Cultural Lines of Conflict
affiliations: University of Trier/ Germany

detail.title: (No) Opportunities for Redistributive Policies? - Voting Behavior and Cross-Pressures Between Economic and Cultural Lines of Conflict

declarations.funderStatement: University of Trier, Germany. Own project as staff member; funding by Chair "Sociology/ Social Policy"

detail.abstract: Growing discrepancies in income and wealth distribution alone do not promote public support for redistributive policies or make corresponding tax and social policy programs acceptable to the majority. Thus, the extent of redistributive policy is less than actual inequality would suggest. There are various explanations for this discrepancy. Research on the relation between economic inequality and established policy ends too soon. There is little analysis of how general sympathy for equality translates into party choice. This paper looks at the interplay between economic and cultural dimensions of political conflict and its impact on voter behaviour. Cultural issues in the second conflict dimension (immigration, climate change) interact with the socioeconomic issue to influence political behaviour. The influence of cross-pressures between socioeconomic and cultural issues on party choice is analysed based on GLES data.

title: Addressing Financial Stability in the Era of Cloud Computing
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Yong Pung How School of Law

detail.title: Addressing Financial Stability in the Era of Cloud Computing

publicationDetails.detailsText: Singapore Management University School of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Singapore Management University Yong Pung How School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the rapid adoption of cloud computing in financial services is transforming the operational foundations of the global financial system and generating new forms of systemic risk. While cloud services offer substantial benefits, including efficiency and scalability, the consolidation of critical financial infrastructures within a small number of cloud service providers (CSPs) has created unprecedented interconnectedness and potential contagion across institutions. This paper analyses from a comparative perspective all the regulatory models that have tried to mitigate the risks created by the reliance on CSPs (outsourcing rules, designation regimes for critical third parties, and prudential capital requirements) and demonstrates that all of them remain structurally misaligned with the dynamics of cloud-based systemic risk. The paper therefore proposes a connectedness and contagion-aware supervisory framework that treats CSPs as macro-critical infrastructures.

title: Copyright: Characters and Adaptation
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University School of Law

detail.title: Copyright: Characters and Adaptation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Elgar Concise Encyclopedia of Law and Literature (Simon Stern and Robert Spoo, eds., 2025)

detail.abstract: The law of copyright in literary characters typically arises when an author creates a new work that decontextualizes or recontextualizes a previously-existing literary character.  This chapter describes how copyright law is applied to literary characters, as distinct from copyright in the text that creates and surrounds those characters.  It considers how U.S. copyright cases approach the meaning of the term “character,” and explores tensions between legal and narratological conceptions of characters as literary devices.  Finally, it discusses the use of characters as intertextual contributors of meaning in adapted works, and addresses some of the pitfalls of current character copyright law in the adaptation setting.

title: A Real-Time Framework for Forecasting Metal Prices
affiliations: University of Milan, University of Milan and University of Milan

detail.title: A Real-Time Framework for Forecasting Metal Prices
detail.abstract: This paper develops a real-time forecasting framework for monthly real prices of four key industrial metals-aluminum, copper, nickel, and zinc-whose demand is rising due to their widespread use in manufacturing and low-carbon technologies. To replicate the information set available to forecasters in real time, we construct a new dataset combining daily financial variables with first-release macroeconomic indicators and use nowcasting techniques to address publication lags. Within this real-time environment, we evaluate the predictive accuracy of a broad set of univariate, multivariate, and factor-augmented models, comparing their performance with two industry benchmarks: survey expectations and futures-spot spread models. Results show that although short-run metal price movements remain difficult to predict, medium-term horizons display substantial forecastability. Indicators of manufacturing activity tied to primary metals such as new orders and capacity utilization-significantly improve forecasting accuracy for aluminum and copper, with more moderate gains for zinc and limited improvements for nickel. Futures and survey forecasts generally underperform the real-time econometric models. These findings highlight the value of incorporating timely macroeconomic information into forecasting frameworks for industrial metal markets.

title: Stock Market Reactions to FDA Complete Response Letter Disclosures: Evidence from Deficiency Types, Firm Characteristics, and Tail Risk
affiliations: and University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: Stock Market Reactions to FDA Complete Response Letter Disclosures: Evidence from Deficiency Types, Firm Characteristics, and Tail Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available data and does not involve human subjects. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We examine stock market reactions to FDA Complete Response Letters (CRLs), regulatory communications indicating that a drug application will not be approved in its current form. Using a novel hand-collected dataset of 222 CRL events spanning 2008 to 2025 across 104 unique pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms, we document economically and statistically significant negative abnormal returns. The average cumulative abnormal return in the [-1,+1] trading day window is -4.34% (t =-3.87, p < 0.001), representing substantial value destruction. Cross-sectional analysis reveals that pre-event stock volatility is the strongest predictor of reaction magnitude, while CRLs citing Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) deficiencies are associated with approximately 5 percentage points less negative reactions compared to other deficiency types. We extend the analysis to volatility shocks and tail risk, finding that larger firms face significantly lower crash probabilities. These findings contribute to the literature on regulatory information events and have implications for investors, pharmaceutical executives, and regulatory policy.

title: Joint Extreme Value-at-risk and Expected Shortfall Dynamics With a Single Integrated Tail Shape Parameter
affiliations: Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research and Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division

detail.title: Joint Extreme Value-at-risk and Expected Shortfall Dynamics With a Single Integrated Tail Shape Parameter
detail.abstract: We propose a robust semi-parametric framework for persistent time-varying extreme tail behavior, including extreme Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). The framework builds on Extreme Value Theory and uses a conditional version of the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) for peaks-over-threshold (POT) dynamics. Unlike earlier approaches, our model (i) has unit root-like, i.e., integrated autoregressive dynamics for the GPD tail shape, and (ii) re-scales POTs by their thresholds to obtain a more parsimonious model with only one time-varying parameter to describe the entire tail. We establish parameter regions for stationarity, ergodicity, and invertibility for the integrated time-varying parameter model and its filter, and formulate conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator. Using two cryptocurrency exchange rates, we illustrate how the simple single-parameter model is competitive in capturing the dynamics of VaR and ES, particularly in the extreme tail.

title: Highly Disaggregated Land Unavailability
affiliations: The University of North Carolina at Charlotte and York University

detail.title: Highly Disaggregated Land Unavailability
detail.abstract: Standard empirical proxies contradict the canonical prediction that supply constraints amplify house price cycles. We resolve this puzzle by constructing the Land Unavailability--Machine Learning (LU-ML) Indices using high-resolution satellite imagery. Unlike existing measures, our indices capture the nonlinear and heterogeneous impacts of physical geography. We document two main facts: (1) physical constraints are a key determinant of cross-sectional price dynamics, driven largely by the intensive margin (steep slopes); and (2) looser supply constraints significantly mitigate the price effects of demand growth, overturning the "null result" in recent literature.

title: On Whether Sex Is Binary
affiliations: University of Oxford, The University of Sydney and University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL)

detail.title: On Whether Sex Is Binary

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Debates about whether sex is binary often proceed at cross-purposes because the term "sex" is used within different discourses to refer to different phenomena. The term "binary" is also used in contradictory ways. So, people end up talking past each other. In this commentary, we distinguish between sex understood as an abstract evolutionary model based on idealized body plans oriented toward the production of gametes, and sex as a way of classifying actual human persons with diverse bodily features for medical, social, or legal purposes. We also distinguish between two different senses of "binary"-one that implies the existence of two mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories admitting of no exceptions, and one that implies the existence of two prototypical categories with overlapping features and fuzzy boundaries. We argue that while sex (in the first sense) is binary (in the first sense), there are other legitimate uses of each term that may be more appropriate-or even, in some cases, more scientifically accurate-given different descriptive, explanatory, or classificatory aims. We introduce a "Toy Factory" analogy to illustrate these points.

title: Financing Fragility: New Threats and Challenges Amid New Risks and Policy Challenges in a Fragmenting Global Order
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Financing Fragility: New Threats and Challenges Amid New Risks and Policy Challenges in a Fragmenting Global Order
detail.abstract: Fragility has become the center in the current development finance discourse as it reflects a multidimensional interaction between high exposure to shocks and limited coping capacity. In practice, this interaction produces recurrent crises, repeated cycles of violence, displacement, and institutional breakdown. Therefore, it concentrates the world's most severe development challenges in a relatively small set of contexts. Currently, approximately 2.1 billion people live in contexts classified by the OECD as experiencing high or extreme fragility, and these settings contain a disproportionate share of the world's extreme poor. Conflict is also concentrated within this group, with a significant subset experiencing active armed conflict, which helps explain why fragile settings have become the primary locus of humanitarian need and a growing share of long-run poverty. Against this backdrop, this article argues that external financing for fragile states is being reshaped by three interacting trends. First, aid budgets are tightening and becoming more volatile, which increases incentives for short-horizon, high-visibility programming and discourages long-term investments in state capacity. Second, allocation and program design are increasingly securitized, as development finance is more tightly linked to risk management objectives such as migration control and regional stability. This shift tends to privilege rapid stabilization claims even where durable progress depends on long-term institutional trajectories. Third, an instrument shift is underway. Donors and multilateral actors are expanding the use of guarantees, blended structures, and other approaches intended to mobilize private capital. Yet these instruments are difficult to deploy effectively in high-risk environments, where weak regulatory capacity and thin fiscal buffers can translate into expensive capital, contingent liabilities, and rising debt vulnerability. The article also argues that current aid effectiveness assessment approaches are inherently flawed and even counterproductive when applied to fragile contexts. Thus, aid effectiveness in fragile contexts should be assessed not by project-level outputs but by long-term system-level trajectories, especially security, fiscal resilience, and durable service provision.

title: Exchange Rate and Oil Price Dynamics on Nigeria's Trade Balance: Evidence from an ADL-LSTR-ECM-MIDAS Framework
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Nile University of Nigeria and Nile University of Nigeria

detail.title: Exchange Rate and Oil Price Dynamics on Nigeria's Trade Balance: Evidence from an ADL-LSTR-ECM-MIDAS Framework
detail.abstract: This study examines how exchange rate movements and crude oil price shocks transmit into Nigeria's trade balance when external adjustment is nonlinear and information arrives at mixed frequencies. Using quarterly trade balance data and monthly exchange rate and oil price series from 2000M1-2025M9, we estimate a unified ADL-LSTR-ECM-MIDAS framework that allows high-frequency shocks to affect trade balance dynamics in a regime-dependent manner while preserving a long-run equilibrium structure. The results reveal strong state dependence in shortrun adjustment. Exchange rate movements exert large and immediate effects on the trade balance during deficit regimes, when foreign-exchange constraints bind, but have substantially weaker effects in surplus regimes. In contrast, crude oil price shocks dominate adjustment in surplus states and operate primarily through long-run equilibrium channels rather than short-run transmission. While nonlinear dynamics are pronounced in high-frequency adjustment, the error-correction mechanism itself is stable and symmetric across regimes, indicating that nonlinearity arises from short-run transmission rather than long-run correction. These findings imply that conventional linear or temporally aggregated models systematically mischaracterize both the magnitude and timing of external adjustment in commodity-dependent economies. From a policy perspective, the results suggest that exchange rate adjustment is most effective under external stress, whereas oilprice-driven stabilization and buffer accumulation are more relevant during surplus periods.

title: Houses for the People, Power for the Gangs
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Department of Political Science, , , University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada and Independent

detail.title: Houses for the People, Power for the Gangs
detail.abstract: Housing policies are designed to reduce housing deficits and provide secure property rights to low-income families. We argue that, in contexts where organized crime is present, large-scale social housing can unintentionally generate territories of opportunity for criminal organizations. We exploit population thresholds that determine the maximum size of a large-scale housing program in Brazil (Minha Casa, Minha Vida-MCMV), together with longitudinal homicide data for all 5,570 municipalities to estimate the causal effect of housing on lethal violence. We show that municipalities assigned more housing units experience higher homicide rates, with effects that are concentrated among populations that are more vulnerable to organized crime victimization, that grow over time, and are stronger in larger cities. Drawing on original fieldwork, we trace how criminal groups invade developments, expel residents, and use housing complexes as bases for extortion and territorial control. Our findings highlight how redistributive policies can inadvertently strengthen criminal governance.

title: Trading Scarcity Credibility: An Equity Index Strategy Based on Monetary Enforcement Regimes

detail.title: Trading Scarcity Credibility: An Equity Index Strategy Based on Monetary Enforcement Regimes
detail.abstract:
Equity markets often respond very differently to similar monetary policy actions,
with tightening sometimes coinciding with rallies and accommodation at times triggering
sharp drawdowns. This paper argues that these divergent outcomes reflect
not the direction of policy itself, but the credibility of the underlying monetary
constraint. We develop a structural framework in which the stability of equity valuations
depends on the variance of scarcity enforcement—the degree of uncertainty
surrounding whether monetary and institutional constraints will be upheld over
time.
The framework implies a sharp regime distinction. When enforcement variance
is low, monetary equilibrium is determinate, discount rates are stable, and
equity prices are primarily driven by growth and cash-flow expectations. When enforcement
variance exceeds a critical threshold, the system becomes indeterminate
and belief-driven: discount rates dominate valuation dynamics, volatility is amplified,
and traditional policy signals lose effectiveness. This regime shift generates
distinct, testable implications for equity betas, volatility term structures, sector
rotation, and the asymmetric impact of policy interventions.
Building on these insights, the paper introduces a regime-based portfolio methodology
that conditions equity, volatility, and real-asset exposures on real-time estimates
of scarcity enforcement credibility. Using a calibrated numerical market
simulator, we illustrate how such a strategy can exhibit convex return characteristics—
preserving capital during periods of monetary indeterminacy and capturing
outsized gains during regime transitions—without relying on traditional factor premia.
For academics, the framework identifies monetary determinacy risk as a structural
driver of asset prices and a candidate priced macro risk factor. For portfolio
managers, it offers a systematic approach to navigating episodes in which conventional
macro indicators and central bank guidance become unreliable, shifting
the investment focus from predicting policy actions to assessing whether monetary
constraints will be believed.

title:
Democratic Resilience in the 21st Century
The Return of Presidential vs. Parliamentary Debate

detail.title:
Democratic Resilience in the 21st Century
The Return of Presidential vs. Parliamentary Debate
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between government system types and democratic stability across 100+ countries from 2000-2023. Using V-Dem democracy indicators, the analysis finds that the effect of presidential versus parliamentary systems on democratic volatility is conditional on economic development. Presidential systems exhibit lower volatility in low-income contexts where executive autonomy aids crisis response, while parliamentary systems show greater stability in high-income countries where institutional constraints and party systems are stronger. The crossover point occurs at approximately $14,000 GDP per capita (PPP). These findings advance understanding of institutional resilience and have important implications for constitutional design in democratizing states.

title: Physics-Based Decline Curve Analysis and Machine Learning for Temperature Forecasting in Enhanced Geothermal Systems: Utah FORGE
affiliations: University of Houston

detail.title: Physics-Based Decline Curve Analysis and Machine Learning for Temperature Forecasting in Enhanced Geothermal Systems: Utah FORGE
detail.abstract:
Reliable temperature forecasting in Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) is essential for reservoir design and economic assessment, yet petroleum-based decline curves and many machine-learning (ML) surrogates do not enforce geothermal heat transfer. In addition, high-fidelity thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) simulation remains computationally expensive.

This study proposes a unified, physics-consistent framework that advances both decline-curve analysis (DCA) and surrogate modeling for geothermal temperature forecasts. The classical Arps decline family is generalized for geothermal use by introducing an equilibrium-temperature term motivated by Newton-type cooling, ensuring finite late-time temperature limits while reducing exactly to the conventional Arps forms when the equilibrium term is set to zero. The extended decline curves are validated against Utah FORGE downhole temperature measurements and then used to construct learning surrogates on a controlled THM dataset spanning fracture count, well spacing, fracture spacing, host-rock thermal conductivity, and circulation rate. An equation-informed neural network embeds the modified decline equations as differentiable internal computational layers to produce full 0-60 month temperature trajectories from design and operational inputs while preserving interpretable decline structure. A probabilistic Gaussian Process Regression surrogate is also developed for direct multi-horizon forecasting with calibrated uncertainty, while a direct XGBoost regression baseline provides a purely data-driven reference. Across the simulation dataset, the extended decline models reproduce temperature trajectories with near-perfect fidelity (median R² = 0.999; median RMSE = 0.071 °C), and the equation-informed network achieves typical hold-out errors of MAE = 3.06 °C and RMSE = 4.49 °C. The Gaussian Process surrogate delivers the strongest predictive accuracy across 3-60 month horizons (macro R² = 0.965; RMSE = 3.39 °C; MAE = 2.34 °C) with well-calibrated uncertainty, whereas the XGBoost baseline exhibits higher errors, underscoring the value of physical structure or probabilistic modeling for reliable geothermal temperature forecasting.

title: AI-Driven Digital Transformation and Organizational Culture Alignment in Emerging Economies: A Review of the Literature and Future Research Directions

detail.title: AI-Driven Digital Transformation and Organizational Culture Alignment in Emerging Economies: A Review of the Literature and Future Research Directions
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of organizational culture in the success of digital transformation and the adoption of new technologies in organizations. The main purpose of this research is to identify the effects of organizational culture on key factors such as innovation, employee satisfaction, change management, and customer experience. Considering the importance of organizational culture in the competitiveness of organizations in the digital age, this research tries to provide a framework for strengthening organizational culture. This research has been conducted using a descriptive-analytical approach. Data have been collected from previous research reviews and qualitative analysis of the findings. Then, using comparative methods, the impact of organizational culture on different organizational domains has been evaluated. This approach has provided the possibility of a comprehensive and accurate analysis of the relationship between organizational culture and organizational success. The results showed that an organizational culture that is receptive to change and flexibility is a key factor in the success of digital transformation. Also, an organizational culture based on innovation leads to the development of new products and services and increases competitiveness. The findings showed that customer-centric culture improves customer experience and builds long-term relationships with them. One of the main challenges of changing organizational culture is employee resistance and refusal to accept new values. This research showed that senior managers play a key role in reducing these resistances and guiding cultural changes. The use of effective communication methods and employee training is one of the strategies that can facilitate cultural changes. Creating coordination between organizational culture and overall organizational strategies is also an important requirement in this process. A resilient organizational culture increases an organization's ability to manage environmental and internal changes and facilitates the adoption of new technologies. This research showed that organizations with values related to learning and innovation have a greater ability to adapt to complex situations. Reinforcing these values in organizational culture is one of the vital requirements for success in the digital age. An organizational culture based on productivity and innovation has a direct impact on the financial performance and competitiveness of the organization. The findings showed that strengthening the values related to productivity and creating an environment in which employees can work with more motivation increases the profitability and competitiveness of the organization. This indicates the importance of organizational culture in creating sustainable and successful organizations. Organizational culture is recognized as a key factor in the success of organizations in changing environmental conditions and technologies. Organizations should reinforce values such as flexibility, innovation, employee support, and customer orientation in their culture. This research emphasizes the necessity of cultural change in order to achieve success in digital transformation and competitiveness, and provides a practical framework for strengthening organizational culture.

detail.abstract: The World Trade Organization’s (WTO) role in international trade governance has eroded over the past two decades, and that trend has accelerated under the second Trump Administration in the United States. The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Agreement) was negotiated during the Uruguay Round to provide baseline standards of intellectual property (IP) protection and enforcement, combined with legalised WTO dispute settlement. This essay explores the continuing role of the TRIPS Agreement in the post-WTO international economic order, suggesting that the fate of the WTO from a governance (including dispute settlement) standpoint, and that of the TRIPS Agreement from a norm-setting standpoint, are largely distinct. TRIPS Agreement standards have become sufficiently embedded in the national laws of WTO Members, integrated into other trade agreements and arrangements, and otherwise referenced as baseline IP standards to have achieved the status of a type of common law, in the sense of a lex mercatoria, that should persist as benchmark standards for intellectual property protection and enforcement regardless of the fate of the WTO as an institution.

This thesis aims to find out what will influence Cambodia's Pension Schemes development and what difficulty Cambodia may encounter on the path next 20 to 30 years through the case study of the U.K., Germany, South Korea, and Thailand. State pension schemes can be a part of primary social protection networks, which reduce poverty and vulnerability in society, especially protection for low-income groups, through social redistribution schemes or tax-based pension universal benefits for the elderly. According to special conditions of employment in Cambodia, around half proportion of employees are engaging in the informal economy, which cannot be covered by state pension schemes effectively, and the authority shall pay more attention to pension coverage, including the significant proportion of people in rural areas. Combination with the case study of the U.K., Germany, South Korea, and Thailand, this thesis finds the fiscal pressure, problem, and reforms of the U.K.'s pension reform experience, which cause severe instability in society; issues on labor force supplementary and participation on female and old-age groups from Germany; the “crowding-out” effect from South Korea’s social protection systems without effective improvement on poverty groups; and increasing pension coverage rate in rural areas to improve household and children literacy with formal education, especially for vulnerable female children from Thailand’s case. These paths are likely to happen in Cambodia.

Therefore, with PEST analysis, this thesis can sort out and distinguish into four dimensions political, economic, social, and technological factors through the latest literature collection to provide a clear understanding of the context of Cambodia's pension scheme and the disadvantage that authority may prepare in advance to provide comprehensive and efficient governance to expand the potential economy of scale with fast ICT development supported by Royal Government. Finally, the tax-funded basis of the universal pension floor will be a critical part of the whole pension scheme. With sustainability, the authority shall expand Cambodia's financial securities market to contain pension reserves with good governance and foster a pension culture in citizens. And this thesis concludes and provides the short-term and long-term recommendations through the context of analysis.

title: Why “The Next Crash” (Projected 2026) Could be Very Different — A Research-Style Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why “The Next Crash” (Projected 2026) Could be Very Different — A Research-Style Analysis
detail.abstract: Global economic slowdowns in 1930, 2008, and 2020 were triggered by sharp financial shocks, demand collapses, or systemic failures. However, emerging evidence from 2020–2025 suggests that any major downturn expected around 2026 may be structurally different. This paper examines six key macroeconomic and technological shifts that distinguish the next potential crisis from earlier episodes. Using recent data from the IMF, World Bank, and IEA, the study highlights persistent low inflation, declining global crude-oil demand, and a rapid transition toward electric mobility and renewable energy. Precious-metal markets remain stable but fully valued, while equity markets show signs of sector-specific fragility—particularly in banking, legacy manufacturing, and fossil-fuel-based industries. Crypto-assets continue to exhibit high volatility, undermining their role as crisis hedges. Simultaneously, accelerated digitalization and automation since 2020 are reshaping labor markets, potentially creating long-term output gaps and structural unemployment. Together, these factors indicate that a 2026 downturn would likely be a “slow-burn structural crisis” rather than a sharp financial crash. The study concludes that traditional policy tools may be insufficient, and economic resilience will depend on structural reforms, energy-transition readiness, and technological adaptability.

Traditional performance metrics (GDP, Gini) are conceptually inadequate, being myopic and focused exclusively on monetary capital. TCF introduces the TimesLife (TiL) methodology, an algorithmic framework that integrates the hidden ethical costs of labor and the economic environment to measure Subtracted Temporal Capital (CTS). The paper demonstrates that the TimesLife Inequity Index (II-TiL) is a measure of qualitative and
structural inequality superior to the Gini Coefficient. The policy implications are immediate, culminating in the proposal of the Temporal Dignity Income (RDT) as a targeted algorithmic compensation for restoring TON ≥ 1.00.

title: Toward Low-Carbon Diets: Exploring the Role of Climate Perceptions and Household Mitigation in Reducing Meat’s Footprint

detail.title: Toward Low-Carbon Diets: Exploring the Role of Climate Perceptions and Household Mitigation in Reducing Meat’s Footprint
detail.abstract: Reducing the meat industry’s environmental footprint is essential for a sustainable food system, yet global meat demand continues to rise. This study investigates the behavioral mechanisms linking abstract climate perceptions and routine household mitigation practices (e.g., recycling, energy efficiency) to sustainable food choices. Specifically, we examine whether routine pro-environmental behaviors act as a “spillover” mechanism or a behavioral bridge toward lower-carbon dietary changes, such as reducing meat intake or adopting plant-based substitutes. Using a nationwide climate survey of U.S. households (2024–2025), we employ an econometric framework to analyze the drivers of these shifts. The findings reveal that climate change beliefs influence diet largely through an indirect pathway, mediated by the diversity of a household’s existing mitigation actions. These routine practices serve as a crucial behavioral bridge, reducing the psychological barriers to more demanding shifts like plant-based adoption. Furthermore, we find that environmental justice values are significant drivers of high-commitment dietary choices, while specific socio-demographic factors remain persistent barriers to change. By situating food choices within the broader context of household environmental pressure, this research provides a quantified framework for understanding how to align individual consumption with ecological limits. The results offer valuable insights for policymakers and food marketers in developing integrated strategies to facilitate the transition toward a more sustainable, low-carbon food system.

title: The 'green arm' of the job: An empirical study on the influence of green work on green practices

detail.title: The 'green arm' of the job: An empirical study on the influence of green work on green practices
detail.abstract: This article examines the relationship between the ecological dimensions of work and individuals’ lifestyles outside the workplace. Specifically, we investigate the existence and scope of a ‘green arm’ of the job, whereby pro-environmental practices at work may foster similar behaviours in everyday life. To analyse this potential spillover effect, we apply matching and regression techniques to data from the 2023 French Ecology and Environment Barometer. Our results show that individuals taking action in favour of the climate at work adopt more sustainable lifestyles than their counterparts in non-green jobs. In particular, green work is associated with lower levels of climate pessimism, greater participation in pro-environmental political actions (boycotts, protests), and more sustainable daily practices (waste sorting, food choices, energy savings, etc.). By framing work as a driver of ecological awareness and practices, our study broadens the perspective on green jobs, challenges uncontextualized and individualized approaches to eco-citizenship, and calls for a closer look at the central role of work and its transformations (and thus of firms) in supporting the ecological transition.

title: The Work of Nations – Labor Footprints and Unequal Exchange
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Geosciences and Environment (GSE), University of Leeds - Sustainability Research Institute and University of Leeds - School of Geography

detail.title: The Work of Nations – Labor Footprints and Unequal Exchange
detail.abstract: In the globalized economy, the benefits generated through labor performed in one country often accrue primarily to consumers elsewhere. How the burdens and benefits of labor time are allocated among nations is an important question of distributional justice with relevance to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 8. We quantify the labor time worked and the labor consumed through goods and services for 99 countries in 2017, accounting for labor embodied in international trade. We show that workers in most poor countries work more than they consume, while the opposite is true for rich countries. Thanks to our large international dataset, we confirm the trends predicted by Unequal Exchange theory, which argues that price differences between countries lead to net transfers of resources and labor from poor countries (where prices are low) to rich countries (where prices are high). We reveal that adjusting for monetary trade imbalances and labor productivity differences has little qualitative impact on the drain of labor resources from the Global South. In general, labor flows from the periphery and semi-periphery to the core, while the relationship between the periphery and semi-periphery is more complex.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a unified dynamic model of civilizational behavior grounded in three slow-moving structural variables: energetic capacity (E), meaning-dependent activation thresholds (M), and accumulated task demand (D). Instead of relying on historically specific mechanisms or deterministic cycles, the framework focuses on how the long-term alignment among these variables shapes macro-scale trajectories of acceleration, stability, stagnation, or systemic reconfiguration.

Energetic capacity captures the biophysical and institutional ability of a civilization to mobilize resources for coordinated action. Meaning-dependent thresholds represent the level of perceived significance required for large-scale activation, conditioning when available capacity is actually used. Task demand reflects the cumulative obligations, maintenance burdens, and structural commitments that constrain flexibility over time. The interaction of these slow variables generates a limited set of long-run regimes and characteristic transitions among them.

By formalizing these components into a single structural architecture, the paper establishes a conceptual foundation for a general theory of civilizational dynamics. It offers a scalable basis for subsequent work on formal dynamical equations, quantitative calibration, and micro-to-macro mechanisms linking individual meaning formation with large-scale social behavior.

detail.title: Virtual Water in Global Supply Chains: Trade Structure, Industrial Composition, and Policy Levers
detail.abstract: Ecological economists and environmental managers increasingly rely on footprint and input–output tools to track how production and trade redistribute pressure on freshwater systems. We provide global evidence on how international supply chains transmit virtual water and how these flows relate to countries’ development paths and structural change. Using the Eora multiregion input–output framework, we construct a matrix of embodied-water flows for 189 countries, 2010-2021, and aggregate it to country-year net virtual water (NVW) positions consistent with national accounts. A simple open-economy mechanism links NVW to trade structure, manufacturing dependence, income and freshwater endowments, generating testable predictions: NVW outflows rise with export intensity and fall with import intensity; reliance on imported manufacturing intermediates is associated with NVW inflows; and renewable freshwater endowments may not predict net-export status when water constraints are slack. Merging the MRIO data with macro indicators, we find strong support for these predictions: exports are positively associated with NVW outflows, imports with inflows, higher manufacturing shares and income with larger NVW inflows, and freshwater endowments lose explanatory power once trade and industrial structure are controlled for. In growth regressions, NVW positions are essentially unrelated to short-run GDP growth, while renewable freshwater endowments are mildly pro-growth, suggesting the absence of a “water resource curse”. The results highlight actionable levers—efficiency improvements, input substitution, diversified sourcing and better disclosure—that can support expansion of water-intensive green manufacturing without systematically undermining development, and offer ecological economics a transparent framework for assessing embodied-water risks in global supply chains.

title: The Total Power Theory: A Thermodynamic Model of Value and Efficiency in Socio-Economic Systems Resolving the Classical-Austrian Debate and Demonstrating Ethics as Emergent Efficiency

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Total Power Theory (TPT), a novel framework that models socio-economic systems through the lens of thermodynamics. The theory posits that power is not a static accumulation of resources, but a dynamic measure of a system’s thermodynamic efficiency in converting energy into sustained, desired impact. We present a formal mathematical equation for Total Power ( ) that unifies concepts from economics, sociology, and physics. This framework offers three primary contributions.

First, it resolves the century-old debate between the classical (objective) and Austrian (subjective) schools of economic value by proposing a multiplicative synthesis, where value is the product of objective quality and subjective utility. Second, it reformulates power as a flow-based efficiency ratio, explaining phenomena that traditional stockbased models cannot, such as the inherent inefficiency of tyranny and the collapse of seemingly powerful systems. Third, it demonstrates that ethical behavior emerges as a property of mathematical efficiency, suggesting that cooperation and fairness are not merely moral ideals but optimal long-term survival strategies. The theory’s validity is tested through computational simulations of three key experiments: the optimization curve of agent utility, the collapse dynamic of aggressive systems, and a competitive tournament of systemic archetypes. The results confirm the theory’s core postulates, P t with the ethically efficient archetype capturing approximately 74% of system resources in competitive simulations, while aggressive and extractive strategies collapse to near extinction. This provides a robust, quantitative foundation for analyzing and predicting the behavior of complex socio-economic systems.

detail.abstract: In 2004, Italy introduced a national program to address heat-related health risks, combining public awareness campaigns, heatwave warning systems, and hospital protocols. Leveraging administrative mortality data and high-frequency temperature variation, we show that the program reduced heat-related mortality by more than 57% on days at or above 30°C. To identify the mechanisms, we exploit the staggered introduction of heatwave warning systems across provinces and show that treated areas experienced substantially larger reductions in heat-related mortality. We further document that information disclosure plays a key role in driving these reductions. Overall, our findings underscore the importance of public adaptation policies that rely on information provision to cost-effectively mitigate the health impacts of extreme temperatures.

detail.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Advance the Research and Development of Orphan Drugs
detail.abstract: While artificial intelligence has successful and innovative applications in common medicine, could its application facilitate research on rare diseases? This study explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in orphan drug research, focusing on how AI can address three major barriers: high financial risk, development complexity, and low trialability. This paper begins with an overview of orphan drug development and AI applications, defining key concepts and providing a background on the regulatory framework of and AI's role in medical research. Next, it examines how AI can lower financial risks by streamlining drug discovery and development processes, analyzing complex data, and predicting outcomes to improve our understanding of rare diseases. This study then explores how AI can enhance clinical trials through simulations and virtual trials, compensating for the limited patient populations available for rare disease research. Finally, it discusses the broader implications of integrating AI in orphan drug development, emphasizing the potential for AI to accelerate drug discovery and improve treatment success rates, and highlights the need for ongoing innovation and regulatory support to maximize the benefits of AI-driven research in healthcare. Based on those results, we discuss the implications for traditional and AI-powered business in the drug industry.

detail.abstract: Digital platform markets exhibit extreme forms of concentration, winner-takes-all dynamics, and persistent path dependence. Traditional economic models often approximate these markets using linear demand structures or comparative statics, which fail to capture the inherently nonlinear feedback loops that shape platform evolution. This paper proposes a unified framework for understanding platform dynamics based on reinforcement mechanisms and discrete-time nonlinear systems. The model formalizes how network effects, learning effects, and algorithmic personalization jointly generate self-reinforcing growth, stabilizing fixed points, and emergent monopoly structures. We introduce a minimal dynamical model that captures the essential structure of platform reinforcement: user adoption increases platform utility, which in turn accelerates adoption, yielding a positive feedback cycle. Even without strategic behavior or exogenous shocks, the system produces multiple equilibria, lock-in effects, and sensitivity to early conditions. All these features are widely observed in digital markets but insufficiently formalized in existing economic theory. The framework also highlights conditions under which platforms transition between regimes of competition, coexistence, and dominance. By grounding platform economics in nonlinear dynamical systems, this paper provides a conceptual and mathematical basis for explaining why digital markets behave fundamentally differently from classical industries. The unified model offers a foundation for future empirical validation, simulation studies, and policy analysis on competition, stability, and systemic risk in the digital economy.

title: Exploring the factors for evaluating the n-minute city concept: A scoping review
